questions.question: Explain why atoms bond, describe what a Lewis diagram shows, and use dot counts to explain why carbon bonds four times but fluorine only once.
questions.expected_answer: Atoms bond to reach a full outer energy level — the stable, low-energy electron arrangement of a noble gas: eight outer electrons for most atoms, two for the smallest like hydrogen. Only the valence electrons take part, so the Lewis diagram draws exactly those: the element's symbol stands for the nucleus plus all inner electrons, and the valence electrons appear as dots placed singly on the four sides before pairing. The unpaired dots are the atom's bonding hooks. Carbon, in group 14, has four valence electrons drawn as four single dots — four hooks — so it forms four bonds, as in methane. Fluorine, in group 17, has seven dots arranged as three pairs and one single — one hook — so it forms exactly one bond, as in F2 or HF. The three strategies for filling the level: two non-metals share pairs (covalent), a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal (ionic), and metal atoms alone pool electrons into a shared sea (metallic).

questions.question: Contrast covalent and ionic bonding using water and sodium chloride: what holds the atoms together in each, what structure results, and how do the properties follow?
questions.expected_answer: In water the bonding is covalent: oxygen shares one electron pair with each of two hydrogens, each shared pair counting toward both atoms' outer levels, and two lone pairs remain on the oxygen. The bonded unit is a discrete molecule, and covalent substances like wax and water form soft or low-melting materials because only the weak forces between molecules must be overcome. In sodium chloride the bonding is ionic: sodium transfers its single valence electron to chlorine, forming Na plus and Cl minus, and the bond is the electrostatic attraction between the opposite charges. The ions do not form molecules — they stack into a giant three-dimensional crystal lattice, every plus surrounded by minuses and every minus by pluses, so NaCl is a formula unit stating the one-to-one ratio. The lattice's attractions run in all directions, giving high melting points; its rigid ion positions make the crystal brittle, since sliding a layer forces like charges together; and it conducts only when molten or dissolved, because only then are the ions free to move.

questions.question: Describe metallic bonding and the three properties it explains, then calculate the relative formula masses of magnesium chloride and sodium oxide, naming the classic error.
questions.expected_answer: Metallic bonding is the attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions — kernels — and the sea of delocalised valence electrons the atoms have all released; the electrons belong to the whole metal, not to any one atom. The sea explains conduction, because the mobile electrons already flow and carry charge and heat; malleability and ductility, because when layers of ions slide the sea flows around the new arrangement and the bonding survives, so metal bends where an ionic crystal shatters; and shine, because the loose electrons interact strongly with light. Formula masses add relative atomic masses with every subscript honoured. Magnesium chloride, MgCl2: 24 plus two times 35,5 — 24 plus 71 — 95. Sodium oxide, Na2O: the subscript sits on the metal — two times 23 plus 16 — 46 plus 16 — 62. The classic error is skimming a subscript, counting one chloride in MgCl2 or one sodium in Na2O; the cure is the three-beat habit — inventory the atoms aloud, multiply each count by its mass, then add.
